catalog_quote: Matbat has five lexically contrastive tonemes. These are an Extra High Fall, a High Level, a Low Rise, a Low Level, and a Fall. ... The Matbat lexicon is largely monosyllabic. While collecting a 300-item wordlist, I have not encountered any monomorphemic words with more than three syllables. Polysyllabic words often have a weak (toneless) initial syllable vowel /a/. In monomorphemic polysyllabic words, various syllables can carry tones. Examples: /kamo12w/ ‘star’, /wu3yte/ ‘sea shore’, /sapu41lu12y/ ‘round’, /bi3mbo121mpu/ ‘butterfly’. Most polysyllabic function words carry the Low Fall allotone of the Fall toneme on one syllable, e.g. /ya21ka/ ‘I’ and /hafo21/ ‘they’, but /po121re/ ‘not yet’. Some function words are prosodically weak, i.e., they are usually reduced or without any prominence – a case in point is the negative marker /po/. There are perceived prominence contrasts in relat…
sweep_summary: Single item in this search of works with stress in the title: Remijsen's 2001 Leiden dissertation (Glottolog 82038), which is already the catalog's deciding source. downloaded the open LOT full text (215 pp., text) to and read the Matbat chapter (ch. 5, pp. 89-103). It confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding: five tonemes, largely monosyllabic lexicon, toneless weak syllables in polysyllables, and the explicit sentence on p. 90 'there is no evidence for lexical stress as a phonological property independent of lexical tone' (repeated p. 121: 'Matbat does not feature lexical stress'). Recommend extending the catalog's deciding quotation to include that p. 90 sentence; no change of source. The Glottolog papuaweb URL is dead; the LOT URL in the catalog citation works. Remijsen 2010 (Pacific Linguistics 618 chapter, already held by the project from the earlier reading) is silent on stress. Remijsen 2007 'Lexical tone in Magey Matbat' (LOT Occasional Series 9) was not in the item list and could not be located via the LOT site or the author's Edinburgh pages (404/403; it would only be a secondary confirmation of the same author's analysis, so priority low.

new_statements.quote: There are perceived prominence contrasts in relation with the lexical tones. For example, in polysyllabic words with only one tone, the syllable with the tone stands out from among the neighboring toneless syllables. Also, in words with two tones, often one seems more prominent to me, e.g. the penultimate one in /sapu41lu12y/ 'round'.51 However, there is no evidence for lexical stress as a phonological property independent of lexical tone. [fn. 51: This is probably due to the fact that my native language, Dutch, is intonational, with high f0 associated with stressed syllables.] [p. 121: It is relevant to note here that Matbat does not feature lexical stress (see Chapter V).]

This is the explicit no-stress sentence from the same source and chapter the catalog already cites; the catalog's stored quote (p. 89-90) stops before it, so the deciding quotation should be extended to include this sentence.

tone_statements.quote: Matbat does not have lexical stress; it does, however, have an unusually rich tone system. Remijsen (2007) analyses Matbat with six tonemes: Low (/1/), High (/3/), Extra-high Fall (/41/), Low Fall (/21/), Low Rise (/12/), and Rise-Fall (/121/). The domain of tonal specification in Matbat is the syllable; while toneless syllables are permitted, tonal specification is obligatory in content words.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation and the the domain quotation sentence are verbatim in the LOT 49 text we hold at the stated locator (ch. 5 sec. 5.2 pp. 89-90, fn. 51; sec. 5.4.1 p. 102). (2) The classification rests on a 2001 Leiden word-prosody dissertation with acoustic backing, by the only linguist to have worked on Matbat prosody; his 2007 revision (held) changes the toneme count 5->6 but restates 'no evidence for lexical stress as a phonological property', and his 2010 sketch (downloaded now from ANU open repository) gives six tones with toneless syllables and says nothing about stress. Arnold 2025 (held in sibling dir) summarises Matbat as an obligatory, non-culminative six-tone system and places contrastive stress only in the Ma'ya branch. Nothing in the literature seen suggests a stress rule for Matbat; 'tonal' (house classification tonal-OR-pitch accent, no stress rule) is correct, with no word stress

sources.note: Matbat is a tone language with five tonemes (Extra High Fall /41/, High /3/, Low Rise /12/, Low /1/, Fall with allotones /21/ and /121/); the lexicon is largely monosyllabic; polysyllables have toneless (weak) syllables, often an initial /a/, and tone may sit on various syllables. Perceived prominence coincides with the toned syllable (fn. 51 attributes the author's impression to his Dutch L1), and the author states explicitly that there is no evidence for lexical stress as a phonological property independent of tone. sources.citation: Remijsen, Bert. 2010. Nouns and verbs in Magey Matbat. In Michael Ewing & Marian Klamer (eds.), East Nusantara: Typological and areal analyses (Pacific Linguistics 618), 281-311. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics. Open whole-volume PDF, ANU Open Research hdl 1885/146766.
sources.quote: 'each syllable can have one of six lexically distinctive tone patterns: Low, High, Extra High Fall, Low Fall, Low Rise, and Rise-Fall ... transcribed /1, 3, 41, 21, 12, 121/ ... Syllables may be toneless, although content words have at least one syllable specified for tone. If the final syllable of a word has the Low Fall (/21/) associated with it, then a paragoge vowel /-o/ appears ... The syllable template is (C)V(C), and a substantial proportion of words is monosyllabic.' The word 'stress' occurs nowhere in the chapter except in the title of the Ma'ya 2002 reference.
